subject: Orson Welles
hook: The War of the Worlds panic mostly didn't happen.
twist: The 'mass panic' was largely a newspaper exaggeration, yet the uproar made Welles famous enough to win the RKO deal that led to Citizen Kane.
mood: 1930s Art Deco radio-age airbrush: chrome, teal and cream, sunburst dials, streamlined speaker grilles, soft airbrushed gradients. Music: slow-swing 1930s dance-band feel at about 84 bpm, muted trumpet, clarinet, brushed drums and upright bass, with a faint radio-static bed.
narration: The War of the Worlds panic mostly didn't happen. On October thirtieth, nineteen thirty-eight, Orson Welles, aged twenty-three, aired a Martian invasion as fake news bulletins. Next morning, newspapers described a nation in terror. But that night, a telephone survey called five thousand households. Only two percent said they were hearing Welles. A rival comedy show was far more popular. So why the headlines? Radio was taking newspapers' advertising money, and papers had reason to call it unreliable. Some listeners were frightened. Historians say far fewer than reported. Still, the uproar carried his name to Hollywood. In nineteen thirty-nine, RKO gave him almost total creative control. His first finished film there was Citizen Kane. Maybe the newspapers' best invention was Orson Welles. Was it panic, or publicity?

captions.instagram_caption:
The War of the Worlds panic mostly didn't happen. 📻

On October 30, 1938, Orson Welles aired a Martian invasion as fake news bulletins. Next morning, newspapers described a nation in terror.

But a phone survey that night found only 2% of households listening to Welles. A rival comedy show was far more popular.

Historians argue newspapers, losing ad money to radio, had reason to paint it as unreliable. Some listeners were frightened, but far fewer than the story says.

The uproar still carried his name to Hollywood: in 1939 RKO gave him near-total creative control, and Citizen Kane followed.
